annotationRationale: The central task is comparing divisor sums. Prime factorization identifies the relevant divisors; the direct-computation alternative additionally uses a finite geometric sum.

review.questionCheck: Doubling the divisors of 384 accounts for every even divisor of 768. The remaining divisors are 1 and 3, so the difference is 4/768 = 1/192, choice B. The statement, choices and key agree; no figures are involved.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: LIVE and AoPS Solutions 2, 3 and 6 are merged into compute-divisor-sums. AoPS Solution 1 is retained through cancel-reciprocal-divisors, with direct cancellation replacing full evaluation. AoPS Solutions 4 and 5 are merged into cancel-doubled-divisors. All useful distinct routes are represented. No shared-bank methods were supplied.
review.annotationCheck: Divisor sums are correctly assessed, with prime factorization supporting divisor identification. The geometric-sum node appropriately appears only in the computation method.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The map d to 2d is a bijection from divisors of 384 to even divisors of 768. Since the only odd divisors are 1 and 3, subtraction leaves 4/768 = 1/192.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Accurately credits AoPS Solutions 4 and 5 as third-party influences. The candidate gives an original, precise bijection argument rather than reproducing Solution 5's loose divisor-sum notation.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The opening explains why doubling is useful, and both directions of the correspondence are justified. Cancellation is fully reconstructible.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: Both supplied nodes fit: summing positive divisors is central, and prime factorization identifies the odd divisors.

methodReviews.mathCheck: Complementary divisors permute the divisor set, proving f(n) equals the sum of reciprocal divisors. The only extra divisors of 768 are 256 and 768, whose reciprocals sum to 1/192.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Correctly identifies AoPS Solution 1 as the reciprocal-representation source and explicitly distinguishes the candidate's subsequent cancellation. Third-party status and basis are accurate.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The complementary-divisor identity is proved at use. Prime factorizations make the two additional terms clear.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: The divisor-sum node remains central after the proved reciprocal reformulation; prime-exponent structure justifies the divisor comparison.
